title: Two ideas for improving GCSE revision
author: Craig Barton
summary: With GCSE maths exams approaching, Barton offers two revision-lesson tweaks picked up on school visits, both aimed at the same failure mode: revision that feels productive while doing little cognitive work. The first targets topic labelling. Building a lesson around a topic students struggled with is sensible, but announcing that it is a Pythagoras lesson removes the very identification work exams demand and produces an illusion of mastery. His fix is to open with the same unlabelled questions and challenge students to work out the topic and articulate how they know, then pair-share before selected students report. The second targets Walking-Talking Mocks, which he grants are popular and can be done well, but which risk becoming a glorified copying exercise crowned by a beautiful completed paper that flatters students into thinking they have learned. Two tweaks follow: mini-whiteboards used throughout to surface the topic, a definition, the next line of working, or the final answer; and a follow-up question from a shadow paper after each modelled question, so understanding is checked rather than assumed from nods and silence.
points: Labelling a revision lesson by topic robs students of the identification step that exam questions actually require, and manufactures an illusion of mastery when they succeed.
Barton's unlabelled opener asks students not just to name the topic but to put into words how they know, which makes the recognition process itself discussable.
He argues a Walking-Talking Mock can be passive even when done well, because a beautifully completed paper is exactly the artefact that convinces students they have learned something.
Mini-whiteboards are framed as a dual instrument - a check for understanding and a check for effort - that also yields data the teacher can act on in the moment.
The shadow-paper follow-up replaces the useless diagnostic of asking whether anybody has any questions, since nods and silence carry no information about understanding.
quotes: A sensible approach is to identify a topic where students have struggled and base a revision lesson around it. For example, students have struggled with Pythagoras’ theorem in a recent assessment, so you decide to compile a selection of questions on Pythagoras for them to work through with your support.

This is all good. But the problem students often face in exams is identifying exactly what topic a given question relates to. Announcing this is a Pythagoras lesson, or labelling the booklet of questions or worksheet as such, robs students of an important opportunity to practise such identification, and can lead to an illusion of mastery where we assume that if they can successfully complete the questions in the lesson then the topic is no longer an issue.
A simple tweak can help. Present students with the same set of questions at the start of the lesson, but with no hints or cues, and challenge them to identify the topic.

These often take place in a hall, with students sitting at desks and a teacher at the front working their way through a paper whilst students copy the work down. At their best, students have an opportunity to try each question first before the teacher goes through it, and the teacher doesn’t just go through the working out but also narrates their thought processes.

As I always say, mini-whiteboards serve as both a check for understanding and a check for effort. They keep students engaged, keep them thinking, give you valuable data to respond to in the moment, and generally improve the impact of the Walking-Talking Mock.

But a much better way is to have a follow-up check for understanding. In other words, you want a question for them to try that is related to the one you have just gone through. This could be presented as a shadow paper that students dip into after each question has been modelled.
